findings.issue_text: Cleanup ticker in pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:77 changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, a likely leftover debugging change that multiplies frequency of all cleanup jobs by 10x

Debug logging at Error level on every batch in xorm_store.go (lines 535, 556, 573), including full ids slices, spams logs on success path and can misfire error-log alerting; should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the ID list

MaxCount cleanup loop (xorm_store.go:565) uses LimitOffset with fetchIDs and deleteByIDs in separate transactions, so concurrent inserts shift the offset window; deleteByIDs returning 0 affected rows for a non-empty batch terminates the loop early while eligible rows remain

CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (xorm_store.go:589) terminates loop on affected == 0 instead of len(ids) == 0, so if a fetched batch was concurrently deleted by another instance the loop ends while orphans remain

New generic fetchIDs(table, condition) helper (xorm_store.go:620-624) builds SQL via fmt.Sprintf string concatenation of condition containing cutoffDate and annotationType, creating a tempting-to-misuse SQL builder; should accept args or restrict to fixed conditions

Building the SQLite ID list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop (xorm_store.go:620-623) is O(n²) in batch size, copying tens of megabytes per batch; use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt

SQLite parameter-limit check (xorm_store.go:617) compares configured batch size against hardcoded 999 instead of len(ids), and there is no equivalent guard for Postgres (65535 parameter cap) or MySQL; guard should be based on len(ids) and per-dialect

fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate WithDbSession calls with no transactional link (xorm_store.go:530-537); the claimed MySQL deadlock fix is unexplained, unreferenced, and unverified since tests don't exercise MySQL

New 40003-row test case (cleanup_test.go:97-110) only exercises SQLite, so the SQLite interpolation branch and the parameterized branch for other dialects aren't both covered; inserting 40003 annotations plus 80006 tags in 500-row batches also makes the test slow

createTestAnnotations (cleanup_test.go:239) assigns explicit ID values, which may collide with sequence/auto-increment state on Postgres/MySQL if other package tests insert annotations; fragile across dialects
Comment at xorm_store.go:614 says SQLite parameter limit is 999, which is inaccurate for SQLite >= 3.32.0 (default 32766); should state the conservative value is chosen for compatibility

goldens.comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: MaxCount cleanup loop (xorm_store.go:565) uses LimitOffset with fetchIDs and deleteByIDs in separate transactions, so concurrent inserts shift the offset window; deleteByIDs returning 0 affected rows for a non-empty batch terminates the loop early while eligible rows remain

CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (xorm_store.go:589) terminates loop on affected == 0 instead of len(ids) == 0, so if a fetched batch was concurrently deleted by another instance the loop ends while orphans remain

adjudication.rationale: In the new implementation, CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags uses untilDoneOrCancelled, which stops when a batch returns affected == 0. However, the batchWork first fetches a limited list of IDs (fetchIDs with a LIMIT in the condition) and then deletes those IDs. If another worker deletes those fetched rows (or makes them non-orphan) after fetch but before deleteByIDs runs, deleteByIDs can return 0 affected even though len(ids) > 0 and there may still be additional orphaned rows beyond this batch. Because untilDoneOrCancelled treats affected==0 as completion, it would terminate early and potentially leave remaining orphans unprocessed until the next run.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New generic fetchIDs(table, condition) helper (xorm_store.go:620-624) builds SQL via fmt.Sprintf string concatenation of condition containing cutoffDate and annotationType, creating a tempting-to-misuse SQL builder; should accept args or restrict to fixed conditions

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `fetchIDs(ctx, table, condition)` does concatenate SQL strings, but the only call sites pass fixed table names ("annotation", "annotation_tag") and build `condition` from internal constants/values: `annotationType` (an internal condition string), `cutoffDate` (an int64), and dialect-provided `Limit/LimitOffset`. There’s no new user-controlled input flowing into `condition` here, so the finding’s implied SQL injection/security defect is not verifiably present. The concern that it’s “tempting-to-misuse” is forward-looking/speculative rather than a concrete defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Building the SQLite ID list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop (xorm_store.go:620-623) is O(n²) in batch size, copying tens of megabytes per batch; use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In xorm_store.go `deleteByIDs`, when using SQLite with `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`, it builds the `IN (...)` list by repeatedly doing `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. This recreates/copies the entire accumulated string each iteration, which is O(n²) time and causes avoidable allocations. The diff also introduces a test case with a very large batch size (32767), making this inefficiency practically relevant in the new code path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: SQLite parameter-limit check (xorm_store.go:617) compares configured batch size against hardcoded 999 instead of len(ids), and there is no equivalent guard for Postgres (65535 parameter cap) or MySQL; guard should be based on len(ids) and per-dialect

fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate WithDbSession calls with no transactional link (xorm_store.go:530-537); the claimed MySQL deadlock fix is unexplained, unreferenced, and unverified since tests don't exercise MySQL

adjudication.rationale: It’s true that `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs` execute in separate `WithDbSession` calls with no shared transaction, but the diff explicitly documents this as an intentional tradeoff (“may under-delete when concurrent inserts happen… cleaned on the next cycle”). Nothing in the diff demonstrates a correctness bug caused by this separation (deleting by explicit IDs remains safe even if some IDs disappear or new rows are inserted). The rest of the finding (“deadlock fix is unexplained/unreferenced” and “tests don’t exercise MySQL”) is about justification/coverage, not a verifiable defect introduced by the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New 40003-row test case (cleanup_test.go:97-110) only exercises SQLite, so the SQLite interpolation branch and the parameterized branch for other dialects aren't both covered; inserting 40003 annotations plus 80006 tags in 500-row batches also makes the test slow

adjudication.rationale: The new test case does create a very large number of rows (40003 annotations + 80006 tags) in 500-row batches, which could make the integration test slower, but that is a test-performance concern rather than a clear correctness/bug defect introduced by the diff. Also, the claim that it “only exercises SQLite” (and therefore can’t cover both the SQLite interpolation and non-SQLite parameterized branches) is not verifiable from this diff alone: `db.InitTestDB(t)` could be configured to use different DBs in different environments, so the branch coverage depends on external test setup not shown here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: createTestAnnotations (cleanup_test.go:239) assigns explicit ID values, which may collide with sequence/auto-increment state on Postgres/MySQL if other package tests insert annotations; fragile across dialects
Comment at xorm_store.go:614 says SQLite parameter limit is 999, which is inaccurate for SQLite >= 3.32.0 (default 32766); should state the conservative value is chosen for compatibility

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new comment in xorm_store.go stating: "SQLite has a parameter limit of 999." However, the same diff also adds an integration test explicitly referencing SQLite >= 3.32.0 and batch size 32767, reflecting that modern SQLite supports a much higher bound-parameter limit (default 32766). So the comment is misleading/inaccurate as written; at best 999 is a conservative compatibility value for older SQLite builds, which the comment does not clarify.
